title: Congress, Rahul Gandhi biggest challenges to democracy: BJP
excerpt: The ruling BJP national spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi on Monday launched a scathing attack on the opposition Congress and Leader of Opposition(LoP) in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi, accusing them of attempting to undermine democratic institutions and create confusion over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Addressing a press conference in Bhubaneswar, Dr Trivedi said the world has been passing through a period of geopolitical and economic uncertainty, but India has emerged as one of the fastest-growing major economies under the Modi government. Referring to the World Bank's 2025 report, he said India has made significant progress in reducing poverty over the past 12–13 years. He said India is making significant advances in artificial intelligence, defence manufacturing and emerging technologies, besides strengthening its internal and external security. However, he alleged that certain forces, both within and outside the country, are uncomfortable with India's progress and accused the Opposition of becoming a tool in their hands."But the manner in which the Opposition is behaving today gives the impression that it cannot stomach India's progress and the country's growing sense of pride. At this juncture, the Congress party itself and Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi have become the biggest threats to Indian democracy," Trivedi alleged. Citing Congress's prolonged absence from power in several states, he pointed out that the Congress has not formed a government in Odisha since 2000 and referred to its electoral setbacks in Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Nagaland and Sikkim for the last several decades. These states collectively account for around 230 Lok Sabha seats, he said, questioning how the Congress expected to secure a substantial majority from the remaining constituencies despite its weak electoral presence in these regions. Explaining the electoral roll revision process, Trivedi said Booth Level Officers (BLOs), appointed through the Election Commission's administrative machinery, are responsible for carrying out the exercise of adding and deleting names from electoral rolls. Political parties, he said, appointed Booth Level Agents (BLAs) to monitor the process and raise objections wherever necessary. Citing the presence of around 12 lakh BLOs and 22 lakh BLAs across the country, he questioned why Congress representatives had not raised objections at various stages of the revision process. He said the revised electoral rolls were shared with political parties at the district level and subsequently taken up at the state and national levels, providing ample opportunities to raise objections. Trivedi also referred to statements by Congress leaders in Kerala and Karnataka, claiming that some of them have acknowledged the need to remove bogus voter entries through SIR.Addressing allegations concerning large-scale deletions from electoral rolls, Trivedi cited figures relating to voters who had shifted residences, duplicate entries and those who could not be traced during the revision exercise. He also criticised the Opposition's protests, including its actions at All India Radio and demonstrations outside the Prime Minister's residence and other institutions. He alleged that such actions were aimed at creating political instability and undermining public confidence in constitutional institutions. Later, Dr Trivedi joined a massive rally in Kolkata at 3 pm under the banner of the "Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy Campaign". It began after floral tributes were paid to the statue of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose at College Square.

title: Nagaland University-led study on AI and heritage preservation published
excerpt: Lumami, November 2 (MExN): A research team led by Nagaland University (NU) has brought together scholars from Indian institutions to explore how artificial intelligence can support the preservation of India's rich cultural heritage, with the findings published in a peer-reviewed journal. The study, published in Acta Innovations, focuses on manuscripts, endangered languages, oral traditions and historical records, many of which are at risk due to aging, damage or the fading of traditional knowledge. The team includes researchers from institutions in Tamil Nadu, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Telangana and Karnataka, a press release received here stated. The researchers developed a framework to evaluate how AI tools can be used in preservation, with the goal not just to digitise items but to ensure that deeper meanings, historical accuracy and cultural context are maintained. They stressed that AI should not replace understanding or community involvement, and should be deployed alongside experts and local communities to preserve heritage while respecting ownership and tradition. The paper was co-authored by Prof Ravi Ranjan Kumar, NU; Major Dr N Kavitha, Vellalar College for Women (Autonomous), Tamil Nadu; Nisha Sengar, PGDAV College Evening, University of Delhi; Dr Sonia Gouri, ABES Engineering College, Ghaziabad; Dr J Lalitha Sridevi, Hyderabad; Kumar Sai Deepak B, Sapthagiri NPS University, Bangalore; and Dr P Deepavathi, Joy University, Tamil Nadu. Highlighting the need for institutions across India to collaborate on research, Prof Jagadish K Patnaik, Vice-Chancellor, NU, said the initiative reflects the growing potential of AI in safeguarding India's rich and diverse cultural heritage. He added that equally important is ensuring such technological interventions respect cultural contexts, community rights and ethical considerations. Elaborating on the research, Prof Ravi Ranjan Kumar, Hindi Department, NU, said a key contribution of the study is a framework that evaluates AI-assisted cultural preservation across nine areas - digitisation accuracy, text recognition, classification, translation, visual reconstruction, descriptive information, cultural context, accessibility and ethics. The framework combines technical assessments with reviews by subject experts and relevant communities. He noted that technical accuracy does not necessarily guarantee cultural accuracy, as an AI system may correctly transcribe a document or translate spoken words while missing historical references, cultural nuances or the significance of a tradition. Expert verification and community consultation are therefore essential, particularly when working with less commonly used languages, unusual scripts, damaged documents and oral histories. The framework suggested that any AI use must include input from the people whose heritage is being preserved, and calls for guidelines on data use, privacy and access. The research identified five key areas where AI could support cultural preservation: printed and handwritten documents; photographs and artworks; oral histories and endangered languages; archaeological and architectural heritage; and folklore and community knowledge. Potential applications include making historical documents searchable, organising image collections, identifying damage to artworks, transcribing oral recordings, translating multilingual materials and creating digital maps and three-dimensional models of heritage sites. The study also highlighted the importance of distinguishing between restoration and reconstruction, recommending the retention of original digital files, documentation of AI-generated changes and clear indication of uncertainty so that users can distinguish original evidence from computer-generated interpretations. The proposed framework could be particularly relevant to India, where historical manuscripts, regional languages, oral traditions and community knowledge represent a vast and diverse cultural record. In the Northeast, it could help explore approaches to preserving endangered languages and documenting oral histories, provided the tools are suitable for the languages concerned and communities participate in decisions about how their heritage is recorded and shared. For libraries, museums, universities and archives, searchable digital collections could improve access for students and researchers while reducing the need to repeatedly handle fragile original documents, the researchers said. The authors recommended piloting the framework across different collections, scripts and dialects to assess its practical value, documenting recognition errors, incorporating expert and community feedback and establishing whether AI-generated outputs are appropriate for their intended uses.

title: Haldiram’s Bets Big on Digital This Diwali, Ropes in Bollywood Stars, Regional Celebrities, Comedians and AI Creators for Its Biggest Festive Campaign
excerpt: From film and television stars to regional cinema talent, comedians, digital creators and an AI creator, Haldiram’s adopts a digital-first approach, supported by print, outdoor and quick-commerce campaigns across key markets. November 2, 2026, : Haldiram’s, one of India’s most loved snack and sweets brand, has gone all out this festive season with its Diwali marketing campaign, ‘Haldiram’s Se Bani Khaas Diwali’. Bringing together personalities from film, television, regional cinema, comedy and digital content, including an AI creator, the brand has taken a digital-first approach to connect with consumers across generations, cultures and geographies. While Haldiram’s has long been associated with Diwali celebrations, sweets and gifting, this year marks a significant expansion in the scale and approach of its festive marketing. The integrated campaign spans social media, creator collaborations, quick-commerce partnerships, print advertising and outdoor media, building visibility wherever consumers are celebrating, engaging or shopping. A Digital-First Diwali Across Entertainment Genres and Creator Formats At the heart of the campaign is an expansive digital strategy featuring personalities from film, television, comedy, food and digital entertainment, each connecting with audiences through a distinctive storytelling style. Across film and OTT, the campaign features Shruti Haasan, Rana Daggubati, Sreeleela, Neha Dhupia, Angad Bedi, Rohit Saraf, Malavika Mohanan and Shriya Pilgaonkar. The line-up also includes television personalities Ankita Lokhande, Vicky Jain, Divyanka Tripathi and Mahima Makwana, alongside filmmaker and choreographer Farah Khan, celebrity chef Sanjeev Kapoor and actor-comedian Aparshakti Khurana. Recognising the importance of regional relevance, Haldiram’s worked with familiar faces from southern cinema, including Rana Daggubati, Sreeleela, Shruti Haasan and Malavika Mohanan, to create culturally resonant festive content. Moving beyond conventional celebrity endorsements, the brand has embraced the creator economy through collaborations with digital entertainers Purav Jha and Aaditya Kulshreshth (Kullu), and content creator Rida Tharana. Haldiram’s has also explored AI-led storytelling through a collaboration with the AI creator Sardar Jappu Singh. With multiple celebrity and creator-led videos, the campaign has established a wide-ranging digital presence across Instagram and YouTube, bringing festive storytelling to audiences through the personalities and content formats they already enjoy. Taking Festive Celebrations to Quick Commerce Extending its digital-first approach from content into commerce, Haldiram’s partnered with Blinkit and Zepto for festive campaigns that bring together the joy of Diwali and the convenience of quick delivery. The Blinkit collaboration brought alive the playful thought, “Arrey, Diwali pe meetha kaun ginta hai? Diwali hai, Haldiram’s toh banta hai!”, celebrating the indulgence that comes with the festive season. Taking the festive spirit a step further, Haldiram’s partnered with Zepto around the thought “Iss Baar Mithai Kam Nahi Padne Denge”, addressing a familiar Diwali concern with a delightful surprise. From November 6–8, 2026, the campaign will offer complimentary mithai and gifts with every Zepto order, adding an extra touch of sweetness to consumers’ celebrations. Haldiram’s also introduced a dedicated “Haldiram’s House of Sweets” destination on Blinkit, offering a focused storefront for consumers to discover and shop for festive favourites. Together, these partnerships bring festive storytelling closer to the point of purchase, making Haldiram’s sweets, snacks and gifting options more accessible during the celebrations. A Strong Multi-Market Presence Across Print and Outdoor Complementing its digital push, Haldiram’s rolled out print and outdoor advertising across key Indian markets under the umbrella theme “Haldiram’s Se Bani Khaas Diwali”. The communication celebrates the role of sweets, snacks and gifting in making festive moments special. Outdoor placements include high-footfall locations across western and southern India, as well as select locations in Delhi. Print campaigns appeared across Bombay Times, Bangalore Times, Hyderabad Times, Chennai Times, Pune Times, Nashik Times, Maharashtra Times, Navbharat Times, Vijay Karnataka, Bangalore Mirror, Sakal, Eenadu and Dainik Bhaskar. Reimagining Festive Marketing While Staying True to Tradition “Haldiram’s has always been an integral part of Diwali celebrations in Indian households. This year, we wanted to take that association to an entirely new level, both in terms of scale and how we connect with our consumers. Our approach has been digital-first, but more importantly, audience-first. We recognise that India doesn’t consume content in one language, through one format or from one kind of personality. So, whether it’s Bollywood celebrities, regional cinema stars, television favourites, comedians, digital creators or even an AI creator, we wanted to be present wherever our consumers are, with the people they love watching and the content they genuinely engage with. We have made a conscious effort to strengthen our regional connect across India, while also experimenting with newer formats and creator-led storytelling. At the same time, our partnerships with Blinkit and Zepto bring together brand engagement and shopping convenience, making Haldiram’s even more accessible during the festive season. For us, the idea is simple: Diwali is incomplete without those little moments of indulgence, sharing and togetherness. And when it’s Diwali, Haldiram’s toh banta hai! After all, Haldiram’s Se Bani Khaas Diwali.” Divya Batra, Vice President – Marketing, Haldiram’s, Making Every Diwali Celebration Khaas With one of its most extensive festive marketing initiatives to date, Haldiram’s has brought together traditional media, digital personalities and the convenience of quick commerce under one campaign. Combining its heritage in Indian celebrations with contemporary content and regional storytelling, the brand continues to reinforce its place in the hearts and homes of Indian consumers. Because when it comes to celebrating Diwali, Haldiram’s toh banta hai!
